summary: Specifies how to use the RSA-KEM Key Transport Algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It lets a sender transport keying data to a recipient using that recipient's RSA public key in a one-pass way. It defines the ASN.1 syntax. It was replaced by RFC 9690.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a secret key to a friend is like locking it in a box only they can open. This explains one way to build that box so messages can be protected.

subtitle: A secure one-pass method to transport encryption keys using RSA public keys.

tldr.problem: Applications need a secure way to send encryption keys to recipients using the recipient's RSA public key, in a way that is provably secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks.
tldr.mechanism: RSA-KEM encrypts a random number with the recipient's RSA public key, derives a key-encrypting key from that random number, then uses the key-encrypting key to wrap the actual keying data.
tldr.outcome: This provides a tighter security proof than older RSA-based key transport schemes like PKCS #1 v1.5. It was integrated into CMS and was replaced by RFC 9690.

today: RFC 5990 is a Proposed Standard in the Internet Standards Track. It has been superseded by RFC 9690. The RSA-KEM mechanism is one option for secure key transport in CMS alongside RSAES-OAEP.

sections.title: What is RSA-KEM?
sections.content:
RSA-KEM is a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) that lets one party send an encryption key securely to another party who holds an RSA public key. The sender encrypts a random number with the recipient's RSA public key, derives a key-encrypting key from that random number, and then uses that derived key to encrypt the actual keying data that needs to be transported.

Unlike older approaches, which directly encrypt the keying data with RSA, RSA-KEM separates the RSA operation (which works on a random value) from the symmetric wrapping operation (which protects the actual keying data). This separation provides a provably secure result in the random oracle model.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of locking the key directly in the box, you generate a secret code, lock that code in the box, then use the secret code to lock the real key. This is more secure because the RSA part is not touching the real key.

sections.title: How RSA-KEM Works
sections.content:
The RSA-KEM algorithm operates in six steps. First, the sender generates a random integer between 0 and the RSA modulus minus 1. Second, the sender encrypts this random integer using the recipient's RSA public key. Third, the sender derives a key-encrypting key (KEK) by passing the random integer through a key derivation function such as KDF3. Fourth, the sender wraps the actual keying data using the KEK with a symmetric key-wrapping scheme like AES-Wrap. Fifth, the sender concatenates the encrypted random integer and the wrapped keying data. Sixth, the sender outputs the concatenated result.

On the receiving side, the recipient reverses the process. The recipient decrypts the encrypted random integer using the RSA private key, derives the same KEK, and unwraps the keying data.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing a secret code in the locked box, then using that code to unlock the real key. The recipient opens the box to get the code, then uses the code to get the real key.

sections.title: Why This Design is Better
sections.content:
RSA-KEM has three key advantages over older schemes. First, the RSA operation works on a random value that has no structure, unlike PKCS #1 v1.5 where the RSA input depends on the actual keying data. Second, the RSA operation is independent of the keying data, so an adversary cannot use the RSA decryption result to recover the keying data directly. Third, the key-wrapping scheme is not limited by the size of the RSA modulus, so keys can be of any length supported by the wrapping algorithm.

These properties lead to a tight security proof in the random oracle model, unlike PKCS #1 v1.5 and other older methods.
sections.plainLanguage: This way is more secure because the RSA part never touches the real key. Even if someone watches the locked box, they only see the secret code, not the real key.

sections.title: Using RSA-KEM with CMS
sections.content:
RFC 5990 specifies how to use RSA-KEM within the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is the standard way to send encrypted and signed messages on the Internet. When using RSA-KEM with CMS, the sender identifies the algorithm with the object identifier id-rsa-kem and specifies which underlying components (key derivation function and symmetric key-wrapping scheme) are being used.

The RFC requires support for at least KDF3 with SHA-256 and AES-Wrap-128. Implementations should also support KDF2 with SHA-1, the Camellia key wrap if Camellia is used for encryption, and Triple-DES key wrap if Triple-DES is used.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is the standard format for encrypted messages on the Internet. This RFC explains how to include the RSA-KEM box-and-code method in those messages.

sections.title: Security Matters
sections.content:
The security of RSA-KEM depends on three factors: the strength of the RSA key, the strength of the key derivation function, and the strength of the symmetric key-wrapping scheme. The RFC recommends matching these strengths. For 128-bit security, the RSA key should be at least 3072 bits, the hash function should be SHA-256 or stronger, and the key wrap should be AES or Camellia.

The RFC also emphasizes that an RSA key pair should be used with only one scheme (RSA-KEM, or signatures, but not both), to prevent vulnerability in one scheme from compromising the other. The random number generator must be of high quality, and implementations must protect against timing attacks and side channels by not revealing intermediate values.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a strong lock (big RSA key), a strong code-maker (good hash function), and a strong key-locker (good wrap algorithm). Do not use the same key for locking boxes and signing letters.
